metaTitle: Ranch & Farm Fencing in Lorena, TX | Brazos Ridge Fence
metaDescription: Ranch fencing in Lorena, TX for 5 to 20 acre homesteads along I-35. Barbed wire, pipe, and game fence with free written estimates. Call (509) 351-8404 today.
heroSub: Perimeter fence for new homesteads and working ranches along the I-35 corridor south of Waco. Free written estimates, real per-foot pricing, and crews that know black clay.
introHtml:
Lorena sits right on the I-35 corridor south of Waco, where old cotton and cattle land is turning into 5 to 20 acre homesteads faster than just about anywhere in McLennan County. New owners out here usually inherit a sagging net wire fence from decades back, a survey with fresh corner pins, and a neighbor's cattle that don't respect either one. Brazos Ridge Fence Co. builds the perimeter fence that fixes all three.

We install barbed wire, pipe, net wire, and game fence across Lorena and the southern end of the county, from the I-35 frontage out toward Bullhide Creek and the Falls County line. Every job starts with a free written estimate with honest per-foot numbers, and we're licensed and insured. Call (509) 351-8404 and we'll walk your property lines with you.

services.title: Barbed Wire Fencing
services.desc: Five and six strand barbed wire on t-posts with braced corners, still the most cost-effective way to close a 10 acre Lorena perimeter. We tension every strand so it holds cattle, not just marks the line.

services.title: Pipe Fencing
services.desc: Welded pipe fence and pipe entryways for homesteads along the I-35 frontage where looks matter as much as strength. Pipe shrugs off leaning livestock and the occasional backed-up trailer.

services.title: Game & High Fence
services.desc: Eight foot high-tensile game fence for landowners south of Waco who run exotics or want deer kept out of a food plot. Built with driven posts and proper bracing for Lorena's open blackland ground.

services.title: Ranch Entrance Gates
services.desc: Pipe entrances, cattle guards, and gate operators sized for trucks and stock trailers coming off the county roads around Lorena. We set gate posts deep and in concrete so they never sag.

sections.heading: Fencing New Homesteads Off the I-35 Corridor
sections.html:
A lot of the land around Lorena used to be one big farm, and now it's six or eight tracts of 5 to 20 acres, each with a new survey and no fence on most of the lines. If you just closed on a place like that, your first call is usually a fence builder. A square 10 acre tract runs about 2,640 feet of perimeter, so small differences in per-foot price add up fast.

We build to the surveyed line, not to the old fence that may have wandered 10 feet over the years. If a neighbor wants to share cost on a boundary fence, we'll write the estimate so it's easy to split, and we'll talk to both parties before we set the first post. That one conversation saves a lot of grief later.

For a full breakdown of what barbed wire, net wire, pipe, and game fence run per foot and per mile, see our ranch fence cost guide. As a rough starting point, 5 strand barbed wire around Lorena usually lands between $2.50 and $4.50 per foot depending on terrain, clearing, and corner count.

sections.heading: Built for Lorena's Blackland Clay
sections.html:
Lorena sits on blackland prairie, and that black clay is hard on fence. It swells when it rains and shrinks and cracks in August, which works posts loose and heaves shallow concrete. A fence that stands for 30 years here starts with how deep the posts go, not with the wire.

Our crews set corner and gate posts 36 to 48 inches deep in concrete, use proper H-braces at every pull point, and drive line posts instead of augering where the ground allows. On pipe fence we weld continuous rail so the fence moves as one piece instead of racking apart joint by joint.

We also plan for water. Fence lines that cross low spots and drainages near Bullhide Creek get water gaps built to break away in a flood and go back up in an afternoon, so one gully washer doesn't take out 200 feet of good fence.

sections.heading: Serving Lorena and Southern McLennan County
sections.html:
Our crews are on the south end of the county every week. We cover Lorena proper, the tracts along the I-35 frontage roads, and the farm and ranch land east and west of town out to the Falls County line. Being based near Waco means we're usually on site for an estimate within a few days, not weeks.

We also build in the neighboring communities, so if you have family land in McGregor, Crawford, or China Spring, one call covers all of it. And if a storm drops a tree on your fence or cattle get out on the highway, our emergency line answers 24/7 at (509) 351-8404.

Every estimate is free, written, and itemized by the foot. If you want a pipe entrance added to the job or a game fence quote alongside the barbed wire number, just ask and we'll price both.

faq.q: How much does ranch fencing cost in Lorena?
faq.a: For most Lorena properties, 5 strand barbed wire runs $2.50 to $4.50 per foot, net wire runs $3.50 to $6.00, and pipe fence runs $10 to $16 depending on rail count. Rocky spots, heavy brush, and lots of corners push the number up. We put exact figures in a free written estimate after we walk your lines.

faq.q: I just bought 10 acres near Lorena. How much fence do I actually need?
faq.a: A square 10 acre tract has about 2,640 feet of perimeter, so figure roughly half a mile of fence. Long narrow tracts, which are common where old farms along I-35 got split up, need more footage for the same acreage. Bring your survey to the estimate and we'll measure it off the actual plat.

faq.q: Do I need to talk to my neighbor before building a boundary fence in Lorena?
faq.a: Texas doesn't force a neighbor to split the cost of a boundary fence, but it's smart to talk before we build. Many Lorena landowners agree to share cost 50/50, and we'll write the estimate so it splits cleanly. Either way, we build on the surveyed line so there's no argument later.

faq.q: How do fence posts hold up in the black clay around Lorena?
faq.a: Blackland clay swells wet and cracks dry, and that movement is what loosens posts over time. We set corner and gate posts 36 to 48 inches deep in concrete and drive line posts for a tighter grip than an augered hole. Done right, a fence in this ground should stand 25 to 30 years without major work.
